name: Parking Bays

plainEnglish.en: White lines that mark out one parking space — your whole car has to fit inside them.

formalMeaning.en: A white line marking, at least 100 mm wide, defining the limits of a single parking bay. A driver must park wholly within those lines, and where the bays are angled to the kerb, end up within 150 mm of the kerb line. Where the road has no kerb, the vehicle must be parked as far forward onto the verge as possible without encroaching on the sidewalk.

behaviour.en: Line the car up so no wheel, bumper or mirror crosses or overhangs a bay line, and pull close enough to the kerb on angled bays. Never straddle two bays or leave the tail sticking into the traffic lane.

commonMistake.en: Learners assume 'close enough' is good enough. The requirement is that the vehicle sits wholly inside the lines, so a single wheel over the line is already a contravention.

testHint.en: Watch for the word 'wholly' or 'completely' in the answer options — that is the correct one. An ordinary parking bay is white, which is what separates it from the yellow exclusive bay.

memoryTrick.en: White box, whole car — white lines, whole vehicle inside.

confidence: VERIFIED: name 'PARKING BAYS', white, 100 mm min line width, the three duties in §7.2.10.1(a)-(c) incl. the 150 mm kerb distance.

name: Exclusive Parking Bay

plainEnglish.en: A bay outlined in yellow with a letter inside a yellow oval — only the kind of vehicle that letter stands for may park or even stop there.

formalMeaning.en: A bay demarcated by a continuous solid yellow line on three sides, carrying an oval marking RM7.1 with a designatory letter. No driver may park or stop inside it unless the vehicle is of the class the letter indicates. The letters are A ambulance, B bus, L loading zone, T taxi, F fire-fighting, R rickshaw, CD diplomatic, MB minibus, SOS emergency telephone, D defence force, P police. At an SOS bay no vehicle may park or stop except in an emergency.

behaviour.en: Read the oval before you switch off the engine. In a loading zone (L) only a goods vehicle may stop, and only for as long as loading reasonably takes. In a B or MB bay only a bus or minibus on a fixed route may stop.

commonMistake.en: Learners read it as 'no parking, but a quick stop is fine'. The prohibition covers stopping as well as parking. The other error is assuming an 'L' loading bay is open to anyone with something to carry.

testHint.en: Colour is the discriminator: an ordinary parking bay is white, an exclusive parking bay is yellow with a lettered oval. Expect a question giving a letter and asking which vehicle may use the bay.

memoryTrick.en: Yellow bay, letter of the day — if the letter isn't yours, drive away.

confidence: VERIFIED: all ELEVEN letters read off the RM7.1 diagram — A,B,L,T,F,R,CD,MB,SOS,D,P. The client omitted R (Rickshaw). Bay is YELLOW; restriction covers stopping as well as parking.

name: Exclusive Use Lane Line

plainEnglish.en: A broken yellow line down the side of a lane means that lane is reserved — only the vehicle painted in it (bicycle, BUS, TRAM or high-occupancy vehicle) may use it.

formalMeaning.en: A broken yellow line at least 150 mm wide, used together with an exclusive use symbol or word marking RM17 and the matching reservation sign. Drivers of any other class of vehicle may not drive, stop or park in that lane. Where a selective-restriction sign is used, the reservation applies only during the hours the sign shows.

behaviour.en: Stay out of the lane unless your vehicle is the class shown by the symbol or word. If crossing the lane is the only way to enter or leave premises next to the road, you may cross it — but only when it is safe.

commonMistake.en: Learners read the broken line as permission, the way a broken white lane line is. Here the gaps are just how the boundary is drawn, not an invitation to use the lane.

testHint.en: Colour plus symbol is the tell: a yellow broken line with a bicycle, the word BUS or TRAM, or an HOV symbol inside it. The lane must end at least 20 m before a side road so turning traffic can cross it.

confidence: VERIFIED: RM9 is the Exclusive Use Lane Line (broken yellow, 150 mm min). CLIENT WRONG: RM14 is NOT a reserved-lane marking — it is the No Motor Cycles marking (§7.2.18). There is no RM9/RM14 pairing. Approved symbols are only RM17.1 bicycle, RM17.2 word, RM17.3 disabled, RM17.4 HOV.

name: Box Junction

plainEnglish.en: A yellow criss-crossed box at an intersection: don't drive into it unless you can drive straight out the other side.

formalMeaning.en: Continuous yellow boundary lines enclosing yellow cross-hatched diagonals, all at least 100 mm wide. A driver may not enter the box-marked area if stationary vehicles ahead mean they will not be able to leave it. Vehicles turning left or turning right may enter the box.

behaviour.en: Look past the box before you move off. If the traffic beyond it is standing still and there is no gap for you on the far side, wait behind the box. If you are turning, you may move into the box and wait for a gap.

commonMistake.en: Two errors. The first is reading it as 'you may never stop here', when the actual rule is about whether you can clear it. The second is missing the turning exception, which is the only legitimate reason to be sitting inside the box.

testHint.en: The correct answer is phrased around being able to leave or clear the box, not around stopping in general — and the turning exception is a favourite distractor.

confidence: VERIFIED verbatim: 'shall not enter the box marked area within a junction if they are not able to leave such box marked area due to stationary vehicles ahead of them, EXCEPT that, vehicles turning to the left or to the right may enter such box junctions.' The client's table garbled this row entirely.

name: No Stopping Line

plainEnglish.en: A red line along the edge of the road means you may not stop there at all — not even for a few seconds to let someone out.

formalMeaning.en: A red line marked along the kerb or road edge. A continuous solid red line at least 150 mm wide applies 24 hours a day. A broken red line applies only during the times shown on the accompanying road sign. In either case a driver may not stop a vehicle next to the line.

behaviour.en: Keep moving. Do not stop to drop off or pick up a passenger, take a call, check a map or load anything. If you need to stop, find the nearest place where stopping is allowed.

commonMistake.en: Learners think a red line only bans parking. Stopping is much wider than parking — bringing the car to a standstill at all is already a contravention, which is why the red line is stricter than the yellow one.

testHint.en: Learn the pair together: red governs stopping, yellow governs parking. Then the second axis: solid means all day, broken means only during the hours on the sign.

memoryTrick.en: Red means don't even pause — yellow only means don't stay.

source: SARTSM Vol 1 §7.2.16; paired sign R217 per §2.4.14.4; NRTR 2000 reg 304
confidence: VERIFIED: red, solid-150 mm / broken-100 mm distinction, duties in §7.2.16.1(a)-(b). RM12<->R217 pairing stated explicitly at §2.4.14.4. NOTE: §7.2.16 contains NO 'except in an emergency' exception (client claimed one) — the real exceptions sit in reg 304; deliberately NOT written into learner prose.

name: No Parking Line

plainEnglish.en: A yellow line along the edge of the road means don't leave your car there — you may only pause long enough to actually load or drop someone off.

formalMeaning.en: A yellow line marked along the kerb or road edge. A continuous solid yellow line at least 100 mm wide applies 24 hours a day. A broken yellow line applies only during the times shown on the accompanying road sign. 'Park' in law means keeping a vehicle stationary for longer than is reasonably necessary to load or unload people or goods, so a genuine brief load or drop-off is not parking.

behaviour.en: Stop next to a yellow line only if you are genuinely busy loading or unloading, and pull away the moment you are done. Never leave the vehicle standing there to wait for someone.

commonMistake.en: Learners treat the yellow line as a free waiting bay. Sitting in the car with the engine running while you wait for a passenger is parking, not loading, and it breaks the rule.

testHint.en: Expect a straight red-versus-yellow comparison: red bans stopping outright, yellow bans parking but allows genuine loading.

source: SARTSM Vol 1 §7.2.17; paired sign R216 per §2.4.13.4; NRTA 93 of 1996 s1 definition of 'park'
confidence: VERIFIED: yellow, solid/broken 100 mm forms, duties in §7.2.17.1(a)-(b). RM13<->R216 pairing stated at §2.4.13.4. The 'brief loading allowed' reading rests on the Act's definition of 'park', not on §7.2.17 itself.
